lesson.title: Linear transformations

steps.headline: A matrix turns an input vector into an output. A map that respects adding and scaling is called linear.

lead.text: Each entry of A v is one row of A dotted with v. Such a map T is a linear transformation: it keeps sums and scaling.

lead.latex: T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) \qquad T(cv) = c\,T(v)

lead.text: The first entry of A v is the first row of A dotted with v. Here A is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 2).

reveal.text: You dotted the first row with v. Each output entry has its own row, and the rows of A decide the output.

workedSteps.text: The output is the first column of A.

steps.headline: Find the second coordinate of A(1, 0), for A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: The second output entry is the second row of A, (3, 1), dotted with the input (1, 0).
Work it out. What is the second coordinate?

lead.text: Take the first row of A and dot it with the input. Here A is $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}$ and the input is (2, 1).

reveal.text: You dotted a row with the input. Doing every row gives the whole output, one entry per row.

lead.text: A game shifts every point one unit to the right: S(v) = v + (1, 0). Test any map by asking where it sends the zero vector.

lesson.orientation: Apply a matrix and distinguish linear maps from translations.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A machine takes a point (x, y). It gives back 2x + y across and y up.

intro.promise: By the end you'll apply a matrix to a vector, and test whether a map keeps sums, scaling and the origin.

recap.keyIdea: A matrix maps vectors by dotting each of its rows with the input. Linear maps keep sums and scaling, so zero stays at zero and the columns show where the axes go.

blocks.text: You found that the first output of A v is 4, read a column of a matrix from A(1, 0), and showed that a shift is not linear because zero moves.

recap.nextHook: Two maps in a row make a new map. Next, multiply their matrices to see which order they act in.

questions.prompt: What across value does it give for the point (3, 1)?
hints: Which value goes in for x, and which for y?
2x means 2 times x.
Work out 2 times the x value, then add the y value.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the numbers instead of using 2x as 2 times x.

questions.onCorrect: Put the input in for x and y and calculate. A matrix map does exactly this for every output entry.

questions.prompt: For a linear map T, which expression equals T(3v)?
hints: A linear map keeps scaling.

misconceptions.feedback: A scalar multiplies the output, it does not get added to it.
Scaling the input scales the output of a linear map by the same factor.

questions.onCorrect: A linear map keeps scaling: scale the input and the output scales the same way.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 2), what is the first coordinate of A v?
hints: Which row gives the first output entry?
Multiply each row entry by the matching entry of v, then add.
Dot the first row with v.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the first column of A. Use the first row for the first output entry.

questions.onCorrect: The first row dotted with v gives the first output entry: 2 × 1 + 1 × 2.

acceptedIdeas: Each row's second entry is multiplied by 0, so only the first entry is left.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zero kills the second entry of every row, leaving the first entries: the first column.

questions.prompt: Why does the input (1, 0) pick out the first column of a matrix?

choices.label: Each row's second entry is multiplied by 0, so only the first entry is left.
The input (1, 0) is always the largest vector.

hints: What happens to an entry that is multiplied by zero?

misconceptions.feedback: Size has nothing to do with it. Look at what the zero in the input multiplies.
Only when the first column is zero. In general the first column is the output.

questions.onCorrect: The zero in the input wipes out every row's second entry, leaving the first column.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$, what is the second coordinate of A(1, 0)?
hints: Use the second row of A.
Multiply each entry of that row by the matching input entry, then add.
The input has a zero in it, so one term disappears.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first column is (1, 3), so the second coordinate is 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first coordinate of the output. The question asks for the second.

questions.onCorrect: The input (1, 0) selects the first column of A, so the output is that column.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}$, what is the first coordinate of A(2, 1)?
hints: Use the first row of A.
Multiply each row entry by the matching input entry, then add.
Dot the first row with the input.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the second coordinate of the output. The question asks for the first.

questions.onCorrect: Row dotted with input: 1 × 2 + 2 × 1 gives the first output entry.

questions.prompt: Is the shift S(v) = v + (1, 0) a linear transformation?
hints: Find S(0, 0) and see where zero goes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. S sends zero to (1, 0), but a linear map keeps zero at zero.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the zero vector. A linear map must send it to zero, and this one moves it.

questions.onCorrect: A linear map keeps zero at zero. This shift sends it to (1, 0), so it is not linear.

questions.prompt: For a linear T, which expression always equals T(u + v)?
hints: Apply the map to both vectors, then combine.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A linear map keeps sums: T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v).

misconceptions.feedback: A dot product gives a number, not a vector. Linear maps keep sums.
Both vectors should be mapped. Only T(u) + T(v) treats them alike.

questions.onCorrect: A linear map keeps sums: mapping the sum is the same as summing the maps.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$, what is the second coordinate of A(−1, 4)?
hints: Use the second row of A.
Keep the negative entry in the row.
Dot the second row with the input.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first coordinate of the output. The question asks for the second.
The sign is missing. The row entry is negative and the input entry is positive.

questions.onCorrect: Second row dotted with the input: 0 × (−1) + (−2) × 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: T(3, 2) = 3(2, 5) + 2(1, −1) = (8, 13), so the first coordinate is 8.

questions.prompt: A linear map T sends (1, 0) to (2, 5) and (0, 1) to (1, −1). What is the first coordinate of T(3, 2)?
hints: Write (3, 2) as 3 lots of (1, 0) plus 2 lots of (0, 1).
A linear map keeps scaling and sums.
Combine the scaled outputs, then read the first entry.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the second coordinate of the output. The question asks for the first.

questions.onCorrect: T(3, 2) = 3T(1, 0) + 2T(0, 1). The two column outputs are all you need.
